Chapter overview

Medieval Tamil literature moves from the Nayanmars and Alvars through canonical compilation, philosophy, epics, court poetry, grammar, commentaries, minor genres, Siddhar writing and the separate Islamic and Christian Tamil traditions.

BhaktiCanonsScholarshipLiterary formsReligious traditions
Period, Scope and Early Saiva Saints

Medieval Tamil literature developed across several dynastic phases and expanded through Bhakti, temple culture, scholarship and later religious traditions.

Period and Scope

Medieval Tamil literature broadly developed between the sixth and eighteenth centuries CE.

Major literary streams were:

  • Saiva Bhakti literature
  • Vaishnava Bhakti literature
  • Tamil epics and Puranas
  • Saiva Siddhanta works
  • Grammar and commentaries
  • Sittrilakkiyam or minor literary forms
  • Siddhar literature
  • Islamic and Christian Tamil literature

The Nayanmars and Alvars produced devotional hymns mainly during the Pallava–Pandya period. Epics, Puranas, grammatical works, commentaries and minor literary forms expanded under the Cholas, Pandyas, Vijayanagara rulers and Nayaks.

Nayanmars

The Saiva poet-saints are collectively known as the Nayanmars.

The traditional number of Nayanmars is 63.

Important Nayanmars include:

  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  • Tirugnanasambandar
  • Tirunavukkarasar or Appar
  • Sundarar
  • Kannappa Nayanar
  • Nandanar
  • Cheraman Perumal Nayanar
  • Mangayarkkarasiyar
  • Isaignaniyar

The lives of the 63 Nayanmars were later narrated by Sekkizhar in Periyapuranam.

Karaikkal Ammaiyar

Karaikkal Ammaiyar was one of the earliest Tamil Saiva poet-saints.

She was born as Punithavathiyar at Karaikkal.

Important works attributed to her are:

  • Arputha Tiruvantati
  • Tiru Irattai Manimalai
  • Tiruv alangattu Mootha Tiruppathigam
  • Tiruvalangattu Tiruppathigam

Her poems describe Shiva’s dance at Tiruvalangadu.

Karaikkal Ammaiyar’s works are included in the eleventh Tirumurai.

Women among the Nayanmars

Karaikkal Ammaiyar is one of the three women included among the 63 Nayanmars.

  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  • Mangayarkkarasiyar
  • Isaignaniyar

Mangayarkkarasiyar and Isaignaniyar are the other two women in the traditional list.

Tevaram and the Three Principal Saiva Saints

Tevaram brings together the temple hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar in the first seven Tirumurais.

Tevaram

The hymns of the three principal Saiva saints are collectively known as Tevaram.

The three Tevaram authors are:

  • Tirugnanasambandar
  • Tirunavukkarasar or Appar
  • Sundarar

Tevaram constitutes the first seven Tirumurais:

  • Tirumurais 1–3 — Tirugnanasambandar
  • Tirumurais 4–6 — Tirunavukkarasar
  • Tirumurai 7 — Sundarar

The hymns were composed as Pathigams, generally consisting of ten or eleven verses.

They were sung according to Tamil musical modes known as Panns.

Tirugnanasambandar

Tirumurai: First three

Birthplace: Sirkazhi

Other name: Aludaiya Pillaiyar

According to tradition, Sambandar received divine milk from Parvati and composed his first hymn at the age of three.

His first celebrated hymn begins:

Thodudaya Seviyan

Sambandar is associated with:

  • Sirkazhi
  • Madurai
  • Pandya king Nedumaran
  • Mangayarkkarasiyar
  • Minister Kulachiraiyar
  • Opposition to Jain influence in the Pandya court

Tirugnanasambandar called Tirunavukkarasar Appar, meaning father.

Tirunavukkarasar

Tirumurai: Fourth, fifth and sixth

Birth name: Marulneekkiyar

Popular name: Appar

He was associated for a time with Jainism and was known as Dharmasena.

After returning to Saivism, he became known as Tirunavukkarasar, meaning lord of speech.

His hymns frequently emphasise:

  • Temple service
  • Humility
  • Impermanence
  • Personal surrender
  • Manual cleaning of temple premises

Appar is traditionally associated with the Pallava ruler Mahendravarman I.

Sundarar

Tirumurai: Seventh

Other names: Nampi Arurar and Sundaramurti

Title: Tampiran Tozhar — friend of the Lord

Sundarar’s first hymn begins:

Pitha Piraisudi

His Tiruttondattogai lists the devotees of Shiva.

Tiruttondattogai became an important source for:

  • Nambiyandar Nambi’s Tiruttondar Tiruvantati
  • Sekkizhar’s Periyapuranam

Sundarar was closely associated in tradition with Cheraman Perumal Nayanar.

Compilation and Structure of the Panniru Tirumurai

The Panniru Tirumurai organises the Saiva canon from Tevaram to Periyapuranam.

Compilation of the Tirumurais

The Saiva canon is known as the Panniru Tirumurai, or Twelve Tirumurais.

Compiler of the first eleven Tirumurais: Nambiyandar Nambi

Royal patron: Rajaraja Chola I

Tradition states that Rajaraja I recovered Tevaram palm-leaf manuscripts preserved in a chamber at the Chidambaram temple.

Nambiyandar Nambi arranged the recovered hymns into the first eleven Tirumurais.

Sekkizhar’s Periyapuranam was added later as the twelfth Tirumurai.

Twelve Tirumurais
Tirumurais 1–3

Tirugnanasambandar’s Tevaram hymns.

Tirumurais 4–6

Tirunavukkarasar’s Tevaram hymns.

Tirumurai 7

Sundarar’s Tevaram hymns.

Tirumurai 8
  • Tiruvacakam
  • Tirukkovaiyar

Both were composed by Manikkavacakar.

Tirumurai 9

Contains:

  • Tiruvicaippa
  • Tiruppallandu

These were composed by several Saiva poets, including Senthanar and Karuvur Thevar.

Tirumurai 10

Tirumantiram by Tirumular.

Tirumurai 11

Contains works of several saints, including:

  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  • Cheraman Perumal Nayanar
  • Nakkirar Deva Nayanar
  • Pattinathar
  • Nambiyandar Nambi
Tirumurai 12

Periyapuranam by Sekkizhar.

Manikkavacakar, Tirumular and Nambiyandar Nambi

These three authors connect mystical devotion, philosophy, canonical compilation and Nayanmar memory.

Manikkavacakar

Principal works:

  • Tiruvacakam
  • Tirukkovaiyar

These works constitute the eighth Tirumurai.

Manikkavacakar is traditionally described as a minister of a Pandya king.

He is closely associated with:

  • Tirupperunturai or Avudaiyarkoil
  • Chidambaram
  • Saiva devotional mysticism

Important sections of Tiruvacakam include:

  • Sivapuranam
  • Tiruvempavai
  • Tiruppalliyezhuchi
  • Tirucchatakam
  • Tiruvasal

Tiruvempavai contains 20 hymns sung during the Tamil month of Margazhi.

Tirumular

Work: Tirumantiram

Tirumurai: Tenth

Traditional size: Approximately 3,000 verses

Other name: Tamil Muவாயிரம் or Tamil Three Thousand

Tirumantiram is divided into nine Tantras.

It deals with:

  • Saiva philosophy
  • Yoga
  • Mantra
  • Ethics
  • Body and health
  • Temple worship
  • Liberation
  • Saiva Siddhanta concepts

The expression Anbe Sivam, meaning love is Shiva, is strongly associated with Tirumantiram.

Nambiyandar Nambi

Nambiyandar Nambi compiled the first eleven Tirumurais under Rajaraja Chola I.

His important work is:

Tiruttondar Tiruvantati

It expanded the list of Saiva devotees found in Sundarar’s Tiruttondattogai.

Nambiyandar Nambi’s work became an important source for Sekkizhar’s Periyapuranam.

Periyapuranam and the Nayanmar Tradition

Periyapuranam established the standard literary narrative of the 63 Nayanmars under Chola patronage.

Basic Facts

Author: Sekkizhar

Other name: Tiruttondar Puranam

Period: Twelfth century

Royal patron: Kulottunga Chola II

Tirumurai: Twelfth

Subject: Lives of the 63 Nayanmars

Sekkizhar was born at Kunrathur and served as a minister in the Chola court.

Kulottunga II is also referred to as Anapaya Chola in literary tradition.

Sources of Periyapuranam

Periyapuranam was based primarily on:

  • Sundarar’s Tiruttondattogai
  • Nambiyandar Nambi’s Tiruttondar Tiruvantati
  • Temple traditions
  • Inscriptions and oral accounts

The work begins with the words:

Ulagelam

It narrates the lives of saints from different occupations, regions and social backgrounds.

Structure of Periyapuranam

Periyapuranam is organised around the pilgrimage and life of Sundarar.

It contains accounts of:

  • Appar
  • Sambandar
  • Sundarar
  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  • Kannappa Nayanar
  • Nandanar
  • Siruthondar
  • Cheraman Perumal
  • Mangayarkkarasiyar
  • Kulachirai Nayanar

It established the standard literary account of the 63 Nayanmars.

The saints came from different regions, occupations and social backgrounds; the work presents devotion as more important than social position.

Saiva Siddhanta and the Meykanda Sastras

The Meykanda Sastras systematised Tamil Saiva Siddhanta through the Pati–Pasu–Pasam framework.

Meykanda Sastras

The fourteen principal Tamil Saiva Siddhanta philosophical works are collectively called the Meykanda Sastras.

Important teachers of the Saiva Siddhanta lineage are:

  • Meykandar
  • Arulnandi Sivachariyar
  • Maraijnana Sambandar
  • Umapati Sivam

They are known as the Santana Kuravars.

Meykandar

Work: Sivajnana Bodham

Sivajnana Bodham contains 12 sutras.

It explains three basic categories:

  • Pati — God
  • Pasu — individual soul
  • Pasam — bonds that restrict the soul

Meykandar is regarded as a foundational teacher of Tamil Saiva Siddhanta philosophy.

Arulnandi Sivachariyar

Important works include:

  • Sivajnana Siddhiyar
  • Irupa Irupathu

Sivajnana Siddhiyar explains and expands the philosophical ideas presented in Sivajnana Bodham.

Maraijnana Sambandar

Maraijnana Sambandar occupies the third position in the Santana Kuravar lineage and is remembered as the teacher connected with Umapati Sivam.

Umapati Sivam

Important works attributed to Umapati Sivam include:

  • Sivaprakasam
  • Tiruvarutpayan
  • Vinavenba
  • Potri Pahrodai
  • Kodikkavi
  • Nenjvidu Tutu
  • Sankalpa Nirakaranam
  • Unmai Neri Vilakkam

Nenjvidu Tutu uses the messenger-poem form to communicate Saiva philosophical ideas.

Alvars, Divya Prabandham and Divya Desams

The twelve Alvars, their collected hymns and the 108 Divya Desams form the core Vaishnava devotional framework.

Alvars

The Vaishnava poet-saints are known as the Alvars.

The traditional number of Alvars is 12:

  • Poigai Alvar
  • Bhutath Alvar
  • Pey Alvar
  • Tirumazhisai Alvar
  • Nammalvar
  • Madhurakavi Alvar
  • Kulasekara Alvar
  • Periyalvar
  • Andal
  • Tondaradippodi Alvar
  • Tiruppan Alvar
  • Tirumangai Alvar

Andal was the only woman among the twelve Alvars.

Nalayira Divya Prabandham

The hymns of the twelve Alvars were collected as the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.

Meaning: Collection of four thousand divine hymns

Compiler: Nathamuni

Period of compilation: Approximately ninth–tenth centuries

The collection is honoured as:

  • Tamil Veda
  • Dravida Veda
  • Dravida Prabandham

Its hymns praise Vishnu at sacred temples known as Divya Desams.

Divya Desams

The sacred Vishnu temples praised by the Alvars are called Divya Desams.

The traditional number of Divya Desams is 108.

Important Divya Desams in Tamil Nadu include:

  • Srirangam
  • Kanchipuram
  • Srivilliputhur
  • Tirukkoshtiyur
  • Alvar Tirunagari
  • Tiruvallikeni
  • Kumbakonam
  • Tirumaliruncholai
Major Alvars and Their Works

Major Alvar works are grouped here for quick author–work, verse-count and temple-association revision.

Mudhal Alvars

The first three Alvars are collectively known as the Mudhal Alvars:

  • Poigai Alvar
  • Bhutath Alvar
  • Pey Alvar

Their works are:

  • Mudhal Tiruvantati — Poigai Alvar
  • Irandam Tiruvantati — Bhutath Alvar
  • Munram Tiruvantati — Pey Alvar

Tradition associates their meeting with Tirukkovilur.

Tirumazhisai Alvar

Important works:

  • Nanmugan Tiruvantati
  • Tiruchanda Viruttam

His hymns emphasise devotion to Vishnu and challenge rival philosophical and religious claims.

Nammalvar

Birthplace: Alvar Tirunagari

Other name: Satakopan

Important works:

  • Tiruvaymoli
  • Tiruviruttam
  • Tiruvaciriyam
  • Periya Tiruvantati

Tiruvaymoli contains approximately 1,100 hymns and forms the central devotional text of the Divya Prabandham.

Nammalvar is often called the chief or foremost of the Alvars.

Madhurakavi Alvar

Work: Kanninun Sirutambu

Madhurakavi’s hymns praise his teacher Nammalvar, rather than directly praising Vishnu.

Kanninun Sirutambu contains 11 verses.

Tradition states that Nathamuni used these verses to recover the wider Alvar hymn tradition.

Periyalvar

Birthplace: Srivilliputhur

Original name: Vishnuchittar

Important works:

  • Tiruppallandu
  • Periyalvar Tirumoli

Tiruppallandu begins by blessing Vishnu with long life.

Periyalvar is traditionally regarded as Andal’s foster father.

Andal

Birthplace: Srivilliputhur

Other names: Kodhai and Nachiyar

Title: Sudikkodutha Sudarkodi

Important works:

  • Tiruppavai
  • Nachiyar Tirumoli

Tiruppavai contains 30 verses, one for each day of the Margazhi observance.

Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars.

Kulasekara Alvar

Work: Perumal Tirumoli

Kulasekara Alvar is traditionally identified as a Chera ruler.

His hymns praise Rama and Vishnu’s sacred temples.

Tondaradippodi Alvar

Important works:

  • Tirumalai
  • Tiruppalliyezhuchi

Tiruppalliyezhuchi is a set of hymns awakening the deity at Srirangam.

Tiruppan Alvar

Work: Amalanadipiran

Amalanadipiran contains 10 verses.

The work describes the divine form of Ranganatha from the feet upwards.

Tiruppan Alvar is closely associated with the Srirangam temple.

Tirumangai Alvar

Tirumangai Alvar contributed the largest number of hymns after Nammalvar.

Important works include:

  • Periya Tirumoli
  • Tirukkuruntandakam
  • Tiruneduntandakam
  • Tiruvezhukootrirukkai
  • Siriya Tirumadal
  • Periya Tirumadal

His hymns praise a large number of Divya Desams.

Manipravalam and Vaishnava Commentarial Tradition

Manipravalam linked Tamil hymn interpretation with Sanskrit theological vocabulary in the Vaishnava commentary tradition.

Manipravalam

Manipravalam is a literary style combining Tamil and Sanskrit vocabulary.

It was extensively used in medieval Vaishnava commentaries.

Important Tiruvaymoli commentaries include:

  • Arayirappadi — Tirukkurugai Piran Pillan
  • Onbathinayirappadi — Nanjiyar
  • Irupattunalayirappadi — Periyavachan Pillai
  • Muppattarayirappadi or Eedu — Vadakku Tiruveedhi Pillai

These names refer to the traditional size of the commentaries.

Manipravala prose combined Tamil and Sanskrit and was prominent in Vaishnava theological commentaries, temple traditions, philosophical writings and explanations of the Divya Prabandham.

The numerical names indicate the traditional size of each commentary. Eedu became one of the most important commentaries on Tiruvaymoli and the Divya Prabandham tradition.

Medieval Epics and Puranas

Medieval epics and Puranas adapted pan-Indian narratives and temple traditions to Tamil literary conventions.

Kambaramayanam

Author: Kambar

Original title: Ramavataram

Period: Generally placed in the twelfth century

Source: Valmiki Ramayana

Patron: Sadaiyappa Vallal

Kambaramayanam is one of the greatest medieval Tamil epics.

Kambar adapted the Ramayana story to Tamil literary and cultural conventions.

Six Kandams of Kambaramayanam

The six Kandams composed by Kambar are:

  • Bala Kandam
  • Ayodhya Kandam
  • Aranya Kandam
  • Kishkindha Kandam
  • Sundara Kandam
  • Yuddha Kandam

The Uttara Kandam is traditionally attributed to Ottakoothar, although its authorship remains debated.

Kambaramayanam is also known as:

  • Kamba Ramayanam
  • Kamba Natakam
  • Ramavataram
Kambar’s Other Works

Works attributed to Kambar include:

  • Sarasvati Antati
  • Sadagopar Antati
  • Erezhupathu
  • Silai Ezhupathu
  • Tirukkai Vazhakkam

Kambar is popularly called Kavichakravarti, meaning emperor among poets.

Villibharatam

Author: Villiputhurar

Subject: Mahabharata

Language: Tamil

Villibharatam is a major Tamil rendering of the Mahabharata tradition.

The author’s father is identified as Veeraraghavachariyar.

The surviving work gives particular prominence to:

  • Krishna
  • Pandavas
  • Kurukshetra war
  • Vaishnava devotion
Kandapuranam

Author: Kachiyappa Sivachariyar

Subject: Life and deeds of Murugan

Associated temple: Kumara Kottam, Kanchipuram

Primary source: Sanskrit Skanda Purana tradition

Kandapuranam narrates:

  • Birth of Murugan
  • Defeat of Surapadman
  • Deivanai marriage
  • Valli marriage
  • Saiva theological traditions

The work is traditionally said to have been presented at Kumara Kottam in Kanchipuram.

Tiruvilaiyadal Puranam

The work narrates the 64 divine plays of Shiva at Madurai.

Two important versions are associated with:

  • Perumpatrap Puliyur Nambi
  • Paranjothi Munivar

Paranjothi Munivar’s version became the more widely known text.

Major episodes include:

  • Dharumi and the golden purse
  • Nakkeerar’s debate with Shiva
  • Flooding of the Vaigai
  • Sale of bangles
  • Carrying earth for Pittu
Koyil Puranam

Author: Umapati Sivam

Subject: Chidambaram temple traditions

Koyil Puranam deals with the sacred history of Chidambaram and Nataraja worship.

In Saiva usage, the unqualified term Koyil frequently refers to Chidambaram.

Periyapuranam — Cross-reference

Periyapuranam, patronised by Kulottunga Chola II, is both the twelfth Saiva Tirumurai and an important medieval Tamil epic on the lives of the 63 Nayanmars. Detailed coverage is retained in Topic 6.6.5.

Court Poetry and Major Medieval Poets

Court poets recorded royal campaigns, patronage, processions and devotional poetry through specialised genres.

Jayamkondar

Work: Kalingattuparani

Royal patron: Kulottunga Chola I

Military commander celebrated: Karunakara Tondaiman

Kalingattuparani narrates the Chola expedition against Kalinga.

Jayamkondar was honoured with the title:

Kavichakravarti

Kalingattuparani is regarded as the earliest major surviving example of the Parani genre.

Kalingattuparani

A Parani traditionally celebrates a warrior who defeated one thousand elephants in battle.

Kalingattuparani describes:

  • Chola genealogy
  • Kalinga expedition
  • Karunakara Tondaiman
  • Battlefield scenes
  • Kali and spirits
  • Victory of Kulottunga I

The work combines history, exaggeration, humour and vivid war imagery.

Ottakoothar

Ottakoothar served three Chola rulers:

  • Vikrama Chola
  • Kulottunga Chola II
  • Rajaraja Chola II

He is therefore associated with the Muvarula, or three Ula poems.

Important works include:

  • Vikrama Cholan Ula
  • Kulottunga Cholan Ula
  • Rajaraja Cholan Ula
  • Takkayagapparani
  • Kulottunga Cholan Pillaittamil

The three Ula works are collectively known as Muvarula.

Pugazhendi Pulavar

Principal work: Nalavenba

Nalavenba narrates the story of Nala and Damayanti from the Mahabharata tradition.

It is written in Venpa metre.

Arunagirinathar

Period: Fifteenth century

Principal deity: Murugan

Associated place: Tiruvannamalai

Important works:

  • Tiruppugazh
  • Kandar Anubhuti
  • Kandar Alankaram
  • Vel Viruttam
  • Mayil Viruttam
  • Tiruvaguppu

Tiruppugazh is noted for its complex rhythmic patterns known as Chanda metres.

Arunagirinathar’s hymns describe Murugan temples throughout Tamil Nadu.

Kalamega Pulavar

Kalamega Pulavar was known for:

  • Wordplay
  • Humour
  • Double meanings
  • Improvised poetry

Works attributed to him include:

  • Tiruvanaikka Ula
  • Chitra Madal
  • Parabrahma Vilakkam
Medieval Tamil Grammar and Commentarial Traditions

Grammar and commentaries preserved linguistic rules, literary interpretation and information about earlier Tamil traditions.

Virasoliyam

Author: Buddhamitra

Period: Eleventh century

Royal association: Virarajendra Chola

Virasoliyam deals with:

  • Letters
  • Words
  • Meaning
  • Prosody
  • Rhetoric

It shows substantial interaction between Tamil and Sanskrit grammatical traditions.

Yapparungalam

Author: Amirthasagarar

Religion: Jainism

Subject: Tamil prosody

Yapparungalam systematically explains Tamil metres and poetic structure.

Yapparungalakkarigai

Author: Amirthasagarar

Subject: Prosody

Yapparungalakkarigai presents rules of Tamil metre in a concise Karigai form.

It became an important instructional text for the study of Tamil prosody.

Nannul

Author: Pavanandi Munivar

Period: Approximately thirteenth century

Religion: Jainism

Patron: Seeyagangan

The surviving Nannul principally deals with:

  • Ezhuthu — letters and sounds
  • Sol — words and grammar

Nannul became the most influential Tamil grammatical textbook after Tolkappiyam.

Neminatham

Author: Gunavira Panditar

Subject: Tamil grammar

Religion: Jainism

Neminatham is a concise medieval grammatical work.

Dandialankaram

Dandialankaram deals with Ani, or figures of speech.

It is connected with the Sanskrit Kavyadarsha tradition attributed to Dandin.

The identity of the Tamil author is uncertain.

Nampi Akapporul

Author: Narkavirasa Nambi

Subject: Akam grammar

It systematises:

  • Kalavu
  • Karpu
  • Akam characters
  • Love situations
  • Stages of courtship and marriage
Tolkappiyam Commentators

Important medieval commentators on Tolkappiyam include:

  • Ilampuranar
  • Senavaraiyar
  • Perasiriyar
  • Nachinarkkiniyar
  • Kalladar

Ilampuranar produced the earliest surviving complete commentary associated with Tolkappiyam.

Senavaraiyar is especially associated with Solladikaram.

Nachinarkkiniyar wrote extensive commentaries on several ancient Tamil works.

Silappadikaram Commentators

Important commentaries include:

  • Arumpada Urai
  • Adiyarkkunallar Urai

Adiyarkkunallar’s commentary preserves valuable information on:

  • Music
  • Dance
  • Drama
  • Geography
  • Earlier Tamil literary works
  • Three-Sangam tradition
Tirukkural Commentators

Traditional accounts refer to ten medieval commentators on Tirukkural.

Important surviving commentators include:

  • Manakkudavar
  • Parithiyar
  • Kalingar
  • Pariperumal
  • Parimelalagar

Parimelalagar’s commentary became the most widely studied traditional commentary.

Detailed analysis of Tirukkural belongs to Chapters 9–16.

Sittrilakkiyam and Its Major Forms

Sittrilakkiyam expanded specialised forms such as Antati, Ula, Parani, Pillaittamil, Tutu, Pallu and Kuravanji.

Meaning

Sittrilakkiyam refers to shorter or specialised literary forms.

These works are also called:

  • Prabandham
  • Chitrilakkiyam
  • Minor literary forms

Traditional classification refers to 96 varieties of Sittrilakkiyam.

Major forms include:

  • Antati
  • Ula
  • Parani
  • Pillaittamil
  • Kalambakam
  • Kovai
  • Tutu
  • Pallu
  • Kuravanji
  • Satakam
  • Madal

These forms became particularly prominent between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries.

Antati

In an Antati, the final word, syllable or idea of one verse forms the beginning of the next verse.

Important examples include:

  • Arputha Tiruvantati — Karaikkal Ammaiyar
  • Mudhal Tiruvantati — Poigai Alvar
  • Irandam Tiruvantati — Bhutath Alvar
  • Munram Tiruvantati — Pey Alvar
  • Abhirami Antati — Abhirami Bhattar
Ula

Ula describes a deity or ruler proceeding ceremonially through the streets.

Women belonging to different age groups observe and praise the procession.

Important examples:

  • Muvarula — Ottakoothar
  • Tirukkailaya Jnana Ula — Cheraman Perumal Nayanar
  • Tiruvanaikka Ula — Kalamega Pulavar
Parani

Parani celebrates a warrior who defeated a thousand elephants.

Important examples:

  • Kalingattuparani — Jayamkondar
  • Takkayagapparani — Ottakoothar

Kalingattuparani celebrates Karunakara Tondaiman’s Kalinga campaign under Kulottunga I.

Pillaittamil

Pillaittamil imagines a deity, ruler, saint or patron as a child.

The child is praised through different stages of infancy and childhood.

Important example:

Kulottunga Cholan Pillaittamil — Ottakoothar

It is commonly regarded as one of the earliest complete surviving Pillaittamil works.

Kalambakam

Kalambakam combines different:

  • Metres
  • Themes
  • Poetic voices
  • Literary conventions

Nandikkalambakam is the earliest major surviving Kalambakam.

It praises the Pallava ruler Nandivarman III.

Kovai

Kovai is a linked sequence of Akam poems arranged according to stages of love.

Important examples:

  • Tirukkovaiyar — Manikkavacakar
  • Tanjai Vaanan Kovai — Poyyamozhi Pulavar

Tanjai Vaanan Kovai belongs to approximately the thirteenth century.

Tutu

Tutu is messenger poetry.

A message may be carried by:

  • Bird
  • Cloud
  • Wind
  • Heart
  • Tamil language
  • Other living or non-living objects

Important example:

Nenjvidu Tutu — Umapati Sivam

Pallu

Pallu literature describes agricultural life, particularly the experiences of a Pallar cultivator and his family.

Important works include:

  • Mukkoodarpallu
  • Tiruvaarur Pallu
  • Kurugur Pallu

Mukkoodarpallu is commonly regarded as one of the earliest and most important Pallu works.

Kuravanji

Kuravanji combines poetry, music and drama.

A typical Kuravanji contains:

  • Heroine in love with a deity or ruler
  • Friend or companion
  • Kurathi fortune-teller
  • Description of hill country
  • Prediction of union

The most famous example is:

Tirukutralak Kuravanji — Trikuta Rasappa Kavirayar

It praises the deity and landscape of Courtallam.

Siddhar Literature

Siddhar poetry combined medicine, yoga, philosophy, social criticism and direct spiritual experience.

Siddhars

Siddhar literature developed through poems connected with medicine, yoga, philosophy and social criticism.

Important Siddhars include:

  • Tirumular
  • Agastya
  • Bogar
  • Sivavakkiyar
  • Pattinathar
  • Pambatti Siddhar
  • Kudambai Siddhar
  • Korakkar

The traditional list of 18 Siddhars varies between sources.

Main Features

Siddhar poems frequently deal with:

  • Yoga
  • Medicine
  • Alchemy
  • Human body
  • Impermanence
  • Self-realisation
  • Criticism of empty ritual
  • Criticism of caste pride
  • Direct experience of the divine

Siddhar poetry generally uses simple language, riddles, symbols and colloquial expressions.

Sivavakkiyar

Sivavakkiyar’s poems criticise:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • External ritual
  • Religious hypocrisy
  • Mechanical idol worship without inner realisation

His verses emphasise the divine presence within the human body.

Pattinathar

Pattinathar’s poems focus on:

  • Renunciation
  • Impermanence of wealth
  • Death
  • Detachment
  • Shiva devotion

More than one historical poet may have been known by the name Pattinathar.

Thayumanavar

Period: Eighteenth century

Associated place: Tiruchirappalli region

Thayumanavar composed devotional and philosophical songs combining:

  • Saiva Siddhanta
  • Vedanta
  • Mysticism
  • Inner silence
  • Religious harmony
Islamic Tamil Literature

Islamic Tamil literature developed epic biography, devotional forms and the Arwi or Arabic-Tamil scholarly tradition.

Islamic Tamil Literary Tradition

Islamic Tamil literature grew through Arab–Tamil cultural interaction, devotional writing, religious biography, epic narration and prose or poetry written in Arabic-Tamil script.

Arwi, also called Arabic-Tamil, uses Arabic script to write Tamil and supported religious teaching, prose, poetry and community scholarship.

Umaru Pulavar

Umaru Pulavar was associated with:

  • Ettayapuram
  • Seethakathi
  • Tamil Islamic epic tradition

Seethakathi is also known as Sheikh Abdul Qadir.

After Seethakathi’s death, the completion of the work received support from other patrons.

Seerapuranam

Author: Umaru Pulavar

Subject: Life of Prophet Muhammad

Period: Seventeenth century

Principal patron: Seethakathi

Seerapuranam contains 5,027 verses.

It is divided into three broad Kandams dealing with:

  • Birth and early life
  • Prophetic mission
  • Migration, struggles and religious service

It is the best-known Tamil Islamic epic.

Other Islamic Tamil Literary Forms
  • Munajat — devotional supplication or prayer.
  • Nama — biographical or religious narrative.
  • Masala — question-and-answer or doctrinal exposition.
  • Kissa — narrative tale.
  • Padaippor literature — accounts connected with battles or religious struggles.
  • Religious songs and Arwi prose and poetry formed important community literary traditions.
Christian Tamil Literature

Christian Tamil literature contributed epic poetry, grammar, dictionaries, prose, printing and translation.

Christian Tamil Literary Tradition

Christian Tamil literature developed through missionary printing, prose, grammar, dictionaries, translations, devotional poetry and epic writing.

Veeramamunivar

Original name: Constantine Joseph Beschi

Origin: Italy

Arrival in India: 1710

He became known in Tamil as Veeramamunivar.

Important works include:

  • Thembavani
  • Tonnul Vilakkam
  • Chaturakarathi
  • Tirukkavalur Kalambakam
  • Paramartha Guru Kathai

He contributed to Tamil grammar, lexicography, poetry and prose.

Thembavani

Author: Veeramamunivar

Subject: Life of St Joseph

Religion: Christianity

Structure: Three Kandams and 36 Padalams

Number of verses: Approximately 3,615

Thembavani adapts the Tamil epic tradition to a Christian subject.

Its title means an unfading garland.

Tirukkavalur Kalambakam

Author: Veeramamunivar

Literary form: Kalambakam

Subject: Virgin Mary

The work contains approximately 100 verses and uses an established Tamil minor-literary form for Christian devotion.

Tonnul Vilakkam

Tonnul Vilakkam is Veeramamunivar’s Tamil grammatical work and treats major divisions of Tamil grammar.

Chaturakarathi

Chaturakarathi is a lexicographical work important in the development of Tamil dictionary scholarship.

Paramartha Guru Kathai

Paramartha Guru Kathai is a humorous and satirical prose narrative that contributed to the development of simple Tamil prose.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

This final topic consolidates canonical positions, authors, works, numbers and frequently confused distinctions.

Rapid Revision
Saiva Canon
  • Nayanmars — 63
  • Tevaram — Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar
  • First three Tirumurais — Sambandar
  • Fourth to sixth Tirumurais — Appar
  • Seventh Tirumurai — Sundarar
  • Eighth Tirumurai — Tiruvacakam and Tirukkovaiyar
  • Ninth Tirumurai — Tiruvicaippa and Tiruppallandu
  • Tenth Tirumurai — Tirumantiram
  • Eleventh Tirumurai — works of several saints
  • Twelfth Tirumurai — Periyapuranam
Compilers and Sources
  • First eleven Tirumurais — Nambiyandar Nambi
  • Royal patron — Rajaraja Chola I
  • Tiruttondattogai — Sundarar
  • Tiruttondar Tiruvantati — Nambiyandar Nambi
  • Periyapuranam — Sekkizhar
Saiva Authors
  • Karaikkal Ammaiyar — Arputha Tiruvantati
  • Manikkavacakar — Tiruvacakam and Tirukkovaiyar
  • Tirumular — Tirumantiram
  • Meykandar — Sivajnana Bodham
  • Arulnandi — Sivajnana Siddhiyar
  • Umapati Sivam — Sivaprakasam and Tiruvarutpayan
Vaishnava Canon
  • Alvars — 12
  • Only woman Alvar — Andal
  • Compiler of Divya Prabandham — Nathamuni
  • Divya Prabandham — approximately 4,000 hymns
  • Divya Desams — 108
  • Tiruvaymoli — Nammalvar
  • Kanninun Sirutambu — Madhurakavi
  • Tiruppavai — Andal — 30 verses
  • Amalanadipiran — Tiruppan Alvar — 10 verses
  • Tiruppallandu — Periyalvar
Epics and Puranas
  • Ramavataram — Kambar
  • Patron of Kambar — Sadaiyappa Vallal
  • Periyapuranam — Sekkizhar
  • Villibharatam — Villiputhurar
  • Kandapuranam — Kachiyappa Sivachariyar
  • Tiruvilaiyadal Puranam — Paranjothi Munivar
  • Koyil Puranam — Umapati Sivam
Court Poets
  • Kalingattuparani — Jayamkondar
  • Commander celebrated — Karunakara Tondaiman
  • Muvarula — Ottakoothar
  • Nalavenba — Pugazhendi Pulavar
  • Tiruppugazh — Arunagirinathar
Grammar
  • Virasoliyam — Buddhamitra
  • Yapparungalam — Amirthasagarar
  • Yapparungalakkarigai — Amirthasagarar
  • Nannul — Pavanandi Munivar
  • Neminatham — Gunavira Panditar
  • Nampi Akapporul — Narkavirasa Nambi
Commentators
  • Tolkappiyam — Ilampuranar, Senavaraiyar, Perasiriyar and Nachinarkkiniyar
  • Silappadikaram — Adiyarkkunallar
  • Tirukkural — Manakkudavar and Parimelalagar
  • Tiruvaymoli Eedu — Vadakku Tiruveedhi Pillai
Sittrilakkiyam
  • Nandikkalambakam — earliest major surviving Kalambakam
  • Kalingattuparani — Jayamkondar
  • Muvarula — Ottakoothar
  • Kulottunga Cholan Pillaittamil — Ottakoothar
  • Tanjai Vaanan Kovai — Poyyamozhi Pulavar
  • Nenjvidu Tutu — Umapati Sivam
  • Mukkoodarpallu — major Pallu work
  • Tirukutralak Kuravanji — Trikuta Rasappa Kavirayar
Religious Epics
  • Seerapuranam — Umaru Pulavar — Islam
  • Thembavani — Veeramamunivar — Christianity
Additional Canon and Religious-Literature Revision
Islamic Tamil Literature
  • Seerapuranam — Umaru Pulavar — life of Prophet Muhammad.
  • Principal patron — Seethakathi, also known as Sheikh Abdul Qadir.
  • Approximately 5,027 verses and three broad Kandams.
  • Arwi — Arabic-Tamil writing tradition.
Christian Tamil Literature
  • Veeramamunivar — Constantine Joseph Beschi.
  • Thembavani — life of St Joseph.
  • Tonnul Vilakkam — grammar.
  • Chaturakarathi — lexicon.
  • Paramartha Guru Kathai — prose, humour and satire.
  • Tirukkavalur Kalambakam — Virgin Mary.
High-Yield Distinctions
  • Tevaram refers only to the first seven Tirumurais, not all twelve.
  • Tiruvacakam and Tirukkovaiyar constitute the eighth Tirumurai.
  • Tirumantiram is the tenth Tirumurai.
  • Periyapuranam is the twelfth Tirumurai.
  • Nambiyandar Nambi compiled the first eleven Tirumurais; Periyapuranam was added later.
  • Sundarar wrote Tiruttondattogai; Nambiyandar Nambi wrote Tiruttondar Tiruvantati; Sekkizhar wrote Periyapuranam.
  • Nalayira Divya Prabandham belongs to the Alvars; Tevaram belongs to the Nayanmars.
  • Andal was the only woman Alvar; Karaikkal Ammaiyar was one of three women among the 63 Nayanmars.
  • Tiruppavai contains 30 verses; Amalanadipiran contains 10 verses.
  • Kambar called his epic Ramavataram; it is popularly known as Kambaramayanam.
  • Uttara Kandam is traditionally attributed to Ottakoothar, not Kambar.
  • Kalingattuparani celebrates Karunakara Tondaiman’s Kalinga campaign under Kulottunga I.
  • Muvarula praises Vikrama Chola, Kulottunga II and Rajaraja II.
  • Nannul was written by Pavanandi; Virasoliyam was written by Buddhamitra.
  • Nandikkalambakam praises Nandivarman III.
  • Seerapuranam was written by Umaru Pulavar; Thembavani was written by Veeramamunivar.
  • Tevaram comprises the first seven Tirumurais; Panniru Tirumurai is the complete twelve-part Saiva canon.
  • Tevaram was composed by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar; Tiruvacakam was composed by Manikkavacakar.
  • Nayanmars are Saiva poet-saints; Alvars are Vaishnava poet-saints.
  • Tiruttondattogai was written by Sundarar; Tiruttondar Tiruvantati by Nambiyandar Nambi; Periyapuranam by Sekkizhar.
  • Nalayira Divya Prabandham belongs to the Alvar tradition; Tevaram belongs to the Nayanmar tradition.
  • Tiruppavai was composed by Andal; Tiruvempavai occurs in Manikkavacakar’s Tiruvacakam.
  • Periyalvar’s Tiruppallandu is Vaishnava; the ninth Tirumurai Tiruppallandu belongs to the Saiva canonical grouping.
  • Tiruppalliyezhuchi occurs in both Saiva and Vaishnava devotional traditions; the author and canonical context must be identified.
  • Kambaramayanam retells the Ramayana; Villibharatam retells the Mahabharata.
  • Kalingattuparani is a Parani victory poem; Muvarula is a group of three royal Ula poems.
  • Nannul was written by Pavanandi Munivar; Virasoliyam by Buddhamitra.
  • Antati links the end of one verse to the next; Kovai arranges linked Akam poems through stages of love.
  • Parani celebrates martial victory; Ula describes a ceremonial procession.
  • Pallu focuses on agricultural life; Kuravanji combines poetry, music, drama and fortune-telling.
  • Seerapuranam is the Tamil Islamic epic by Umaru Pulavar; Thembavani is the Christian Tamil epic by Veeramamunivar.
  • Umaru Pulavar belongs to Islamic Tamil literature; Veeramamunivar belongs to Christian Tamil literary history.
  • Andal was the only woman Alvar; Karaikkal Ammaiyar was one of the earliest Saiva poet-saints and one of three women among the Nayanmars.
